prompt: Against whom does encryption at rest protect the clinic's records?
hint: Think of the two rows of the table.

choices.text: Against anybody who reaches the bytes around the service, such as a stolen disk or a misdirected backup
choices.why: Right. What they hold is ciphertext without the key.

choices.text: Against a stranger reading through a public bucket policy
choices.why: The lab showed the opposite: S3 decrypted the record for the anonymous request.

choices.text: Against a user whose policy allows reading the bucket
choices.why: The service decrypts for whoever it is told to answer; that is a question of permissions.

choices.text: Against everybody: it makes the data unreadable to anyone but the owner
choices.why: That is the checkbox picture the section opens by correcting.

prompt: In the lab, an object stored with `AES256` was served to an anonymous `curl` once a bucket policy allowed everybody to read. What went wrong with the encryption?
hint: Where did the decryption happen, and who asked for it?

choices.text: The key was too short to resist a stranger
choices.why: Nothing was broken; nobody attacked the cipher.

choices.text: Nothing: S3 decrypted it for a request the policy allowed
choices.why: Right. Encryption did its job on the disk; the policy decided who was answered.

choices.text: moto ignores encryption, and AWS would have refused the request because the object is encrypted
choices.why: For an object under S3's own key AWS answers the same way; the lesson says so beside the transcript.

choices.text: The object was encrypted after the policy was attached, so it was still plain
choices.why: It was stored encrypted at upload, as `AES256` said, before any policy existed.

prompt: Since January 2023, what does AWS do with a new object in S3 when nobody asks for encryption?
hint: moto does not reproduce this default.

choices.text: Stores it in plain text, as before
choices.why: That changed in January 2023.

choices.text: Refuses the upload until a key is named
choices.why: No upload is refused for lack of a key.

choices.text: Encrypts it anyway, under S3's own key
choices.why: Right, which is why the checkbox is always ticked and proves so little.

choices.text: Encrypts it with a customer managed key created for the account
choices.why: No customer managed key is ever created for you; you create those.

prompt: Match each kind of key to what is true of it.
hint: The table of three kinds.

pairs.right: invisible to you, and its use is not logged in your account
named like `aws/s3`; you can read its policy, not change it
its key policy is written by the clinic, and it can be deleted

right_distractors: its key material is kept outside KMS

prompt: The default key policy allows `kms:*` to `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root`. What does that principal mean?
hint: It is not a person.

choices.text: The account's root user, and nobody else
choices.why: It looks like that and is not: it delegates to IAM.

choices.text: The account, which hands the decision to IAM policies
choices.why: Right. Any identity whose IAM policy allows the action on this key may perform it.

choices.text: Every AWS account, since it ends in `root`
choices.why: It names one account, `123456789012`.

choices.text: The KMS service itself, so it can rotate the key on schedule
choices.why: Rotation needs no permission in the key policy.

prompt: The clinic rewrites a key's policy so that it names only the records application's role, with no statement for the account. An administrator with `AdministratorAccess` asks the key to decrypt. What happens on AWS?
hint: No IAM policy grants use of a key unless the key policy allows it.

choices.text: It decrypts, because `AdministratorAccess` allows every action on every resource
choices.why: Not for a KMS key whose policy no longer delegates to the account.

choices.text: It is refused
choices.why: Right. The key policy decides first, and it names only the application.

choices.text: It decrypts, but CloudTrail flags it as an override
choices.why: There is no override; the request is refused.

choices.text: It depends on whether the administrator also has MFA
choices.why: Nothing in that policy mentions MFA.

prompt: Why did the lab keep the key's id in `k` instead of always using `alias/clinic-records`?
hint: Not every call accepts an alias.

choices.text: Because aliases expire after an hour
choices.why: An alias lasts until it is deleted.

choices.text: moto does not support aliases at all
choices.why: `describe-key` and `encrypt` took the alias in the lab.

choices.text: Calls that administer a key, like `get-key-policy`, take its id or ARN and refuse the alias
choices.why: Right, in AWS as in moto.

choices.text: Using the alias would create a second key
choices.why: An alias only points at a key.

prompt: With a customer managed key as the bucket's default, which two permissions does reading a record take on AWS?
hint: One on the bucket, one on the key.

choices.text: `s3:GetObject` and `kms:Decrypt`
choices.why: Right. Missing either one, the request is refused.

choices.text: `s3:GetObject` and `kms:Encrypt`
choices.why: Reading needs decryption, not encryption.

choices.text: `s3:ListBucket` and `s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration`
choices.why: Neither of those touches the key.

choices.text: `kms:Decrypt` and `kms:GenerateDataKey`
choices.why: That leaves out the bucket, and generating a key is for writing.

prompt: bia has `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess` and nothing on the key. In the lab, `aws s3 cp` of the record printed it. What would AWS have done?
hint: Which half of this did moto judge?

choices.text: Printed it too, since S3 decrypts for anyone allowed to read the bucket
choices.why: That is true of S3's own key; with a customer managed key, KMS is asked on bia's behalf.

choices.text: Refused it with `AccessDenied`, because KMS refuses to decrypt for bia
choices.why: Right, from the documentation; moto did refuse her direct `kms decrypt`.

choices.text: Returned the ciphertext, since she may read the object but not decrypt it
choices.why: S3 never hands out the stored ciphertext; the read is refused.

choices.text: Asked her for MFA before decrypting
choices.why: No such step exists here.

prompt: A bucket policy grants `s3:GetObject` to `"Principal": "*"` on a bucket whose objects are all under a customer managed KMS key. According to AWS's documentation, what does an anonymous request get?
hint: KMS needs an identity to authorise.

choices.text: The object, decrypted, like any public object
choices.why: That is what moto did, and what S3's own key would do; not a KMS key.

choices.text: The object still encrypted, since the key was not used
choices.why: S3 never returns stored ciphertext to a reader.

choices.text: A refusal: objects under a KMS key are read only by requests signed with Signature Version 4
choices.why: Right. Not run here, because moto serves it.

choices.text: A redirect to a presigned URL valid for one hour
choices.why: S3 does not generate links on anybody's behalf.

prompt: Which of these did moto judge exactly as AWS would in the section on two locks? Choose all that apply.
hint: One went its own way.

choices.text: The `test` key refused once checking was on
choices.why: Right: `InvalidClientTokenId` on the fourth request.

choices.text: bia's direct `kms decrypt` refused for lack of `kms:Decrypt`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: bia's `aws s3 cp` of the record under the clinic's key
choices.why: moto served it; AWS would refuse it.

choices.text: The upload going in as `aws:kms` without naming the key
choices.why: Right: the bucket's default encryption applied it.

prompt: Why does S3 not send each object to KMS to be encrypted?
hint: The lab hit the limit with 5000 bytes.

choices.text: KMS takes at most 4096 bytes of plain text per request
choices.why: Right. So KMS encrypts small data keys, and those encrypt the data.

choices.text: Because KMS is in another region and the traffic would cost too much
choices.why: KMS is regional, in the same region; the reason is the size limit.

choices.text: S3 has no permission to call KMS
choices.why: S3 calls KMS on the caller's behalf for every read.

choices.text: KMS only encrypts passwords, by policy
choices.why: It encrypts any data up to its size limit.

prompt: Put the steps a service takes to write and then read an object with envelope encryption in order.
hint: The plain data key is erased before anything is stored.
items: ask KMS for a data key, in plain text and encrypted
encrypt the data locally with the plain data key
erase the plain data key from memory
store the encrypted data key beside the encrypted data
send the encrypted data key to KMS to read the object back
trap: Storing before erasing is the slip: the plain key must never reach the disk.

prompt: `generate-data-key` with `AES_256` returned a plain key of 44 base64 characters. How many bytes is the key?
hint: 256 bits.

prompt: `aws kms decrypt` in the lab named no key, and KMS still answered with the key's ARN. How did it know which key?
hint: Look inside the ciphertext, not the command.

choices.text: It tried every key in the account until one worked
choices.why: Nothing is tried; the answer is in the ciphertext.

choices.text: The ciphertext carries a reference to the key that made it
choices.why: Right. moto writes it as the key id in clear; AWS's format is its own.

choices.text: The alias `alias/clinic-records` is the account's default key and is used for every decrypt
choices.why: There is no account-wide default key for decrypt.

choices.text: The command line read it from `env.sh`
choices.why: `env.sh` holds no key id.

prompt: Why does every read of an object under a customer managed key give the clinic a chance to refuse, while reads under S3's own key give none?
hint: Count who is asked at read time.

choices.text: The data key is sent back to KMS in the caller's name on each read, and the key policy can say no
choices.why: Right. With S3's own key there is no policy of yours to ask.

choices.text: S3's own key is weaker and anybody can break it
choices.why: Both use AES-256; the difference is who decides.

choices.text: Customer managed keys rotate every hour
choices.why: Rotation is yearly by default, and it is not what refuses a read.

choices.text: Objects under S3's own key are never encrypted
choices.why: They are encrypted; S3 just decrypts them for anybody it serves.

prompt: The clinic suspects its key may have been used by an attacker. A colleague proposes rotating it. What does the lesson say?
hint: What does rotation keep?

choices.text: Rotation re-encrypts everything, so the attacker's copies become useless
choices.why: Rotation re-encrypts nothing; older material is kept so old ciphertext still decrypts.

choices.text: Wrong tool: whoever used the key still decrypts everything made before; look at who is allowed to use it
choices.why: Right. A compromise is a question for the key policy and IAM.

choices.text: Rotation is the right answer, and it must be done every day
choices.why: Rotation answers age, not compromise.

choices.text: Delete the key at once, since deletion is immediate
choices.why: Deletion waits 7 to 30 days, and it would make the clinic's own data unreadable.

prompt: After `disable-key`, moto still decrypted the note. What does AWS do with a request to a disabled key?
hint: An exception named after the state.

choices.text: Decrypts it and logs a warning
choices.why: It refuses.

choices.text: Refuses it with `DisabledException`
choices.why: Right, from KMS's documentation; not run here.

choices.text: Refuses it with `AccessDenied`, as with a missing permission
choices.why: The refusal names the key's state, not a permission.

choices.text: Enables the key again automatically for the request
choices.why: A key is enabled only by `enable-key`.

prompt: How many days does AWS wait before deleting a KMS key when `schedule-key-deletion` is given no waiting period?
hint: The date the lab printed was this many days on.

prompt: Which calls on a key does the lesson say deserve an alarm of their own? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two make the data unreadable to the clinic, one readable to somebody else.

choices.text: `DisableKey`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `ScheduleKeyDeletion`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `PutKeyPolicy`
choices.why: Right: it can make the records readable to somebody else.

choices.text: `Decrypt`
choices.why: Every read is one; an alarm on it would ring all day.

choices.text: `GetKeyRotationStatus`
choices.why: Reading a setting changes nothing.

prompt: A key is cancelled out of `PendingDeletion` with `cancel-key-deletion`. In what state is it left, on AWS as in the lab?
hint: Somebody has to decide to switch it back on.

choices.text: `Enabled`, as it was before the deletion was scheduled
choices.why: Cancelling does not enable it.

choices.text: `PendingDeletion`, until the waiting period ends
choices.why: Cancelling ends the pending deletion.

choices.text: `Disabled`
choices.why: Right. The lab printed it after the cancel.

choices.text: Deleted, because a cancellation only stops the timer
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; the key survives, disabled.

prompt: The lab's `env.sh` points at `http://localhost:4567`, plain HTTP. Why is that acceptable there?
hint: Where does the traffic go?

choices.text: Because moto encrypts its answers in a format of its own
choices.why: moto answers in plain HTTP.

choices.text: Because the `test` keys are not secret
choices.why: True, but the same URL pointed elsewhere would leak real keys; the reason is where the traffic goes.

choices.text: The traffic never leaves this computer
choices.why: Right. Pointed at another machine, the same setting would send requests in the open.

choices.text: Because AWS's endpoints also accept plain HTTP
choices.why: AWS's API endpoints answer over HTTPS.

prompt: The condition key a bucket policy uses to refuse requests that did not arrive over TLS is `aws:___`.
hint: It is `false` when the request came without TLS.

prompt: The TLS-only policy lists `arn:aws:s3:::clinic-records` and `arn:aws:s3:::clinic-records/*`. What would be left unprotected if it listed only the first?
hint: An ARN without `/*` matches only the bucket.

choices.text: Nothing: the bucket's ARN covers everything in it
choices.why: It does not; object actions are on the objects' ARNs.

choices.text: Requests for the objects, such as `GetObject`
choices.why: Right, which are the requests that carry the records.

choices.text: Requests from administrators, who are exempt from `Deny`
choices.why: Nobody is exempt from an explicit `Deny` with `Principal` `*`.

choices.text: Only listing the bucket's contents over plain HTTP
choices.why: Listing is a bucket action, which the first ARN does cover.
